body.heading: Same substance, new arrangement
paragraphs: Stir sugar into hot tea and it disappears — but taste the tea and the sugar is obviously still there, unchanged. Nothing new has been made; the sugar crystals have simply spread out among the water molecules. Changes like this, which alter how a substance looks, where it is, or what state it is in, are physical changes.

Physical changes are usually easy to reverse. Evaporate the water and the sugar comes back. Melt a candle and the wax can be re-formed. Cut, crush, bend, dissolve, melt, freeze — the substance's particles stay exactly what they were throughout, just rearranged.

body.heading: New substance, no easy way back
paragraphs: Burn that same sugar and the story is different. It blackens, smokes and turns into carbon, water vapour and gases with new smells and new properties. No amount of cooling will give you the sugar back, because its atoms have been rearranged into different substances. That is a chemical change.

The reliable test is to ask: has a new substance formed? Colour changes, fizzing, heating up and hard-to-reverse results are strong clues. Toasting bread, cooking an egg, souring milk and rusting iron are all chemical changes — the kitchen and the garden are full of them.

body.heading: Both at once, all the time
paragraphs: Real life rarely separates the two neatly. Eating dinner uses both in sequence: chewing is a physical change that chops food into smaller pieces, then enzymes in your digestive system carry out chemical changes that break the pieces into new substances your body can absorb.

Recycling plants exploit the difference. Melting aluminium cans is a physical change, so the metal can be reshaped again and again without loss. Burning rubbish is a chemical change — useful for releasing energy, but the materials themselves are gone for good.

description: Stirring sugar into tea is a physical change you can undo; burning the sugar is a chemical change that cannot be reversed.
